entries.topicDescription: Apple's declarative UI framework for building interfaces across all platforms.

tips.title: Views are structs — cheap and disposable
tips.content:
In SwiftUI, every view is a lightweight struct that conforms
to the View protocol. The framework creates and destroys
them freely during every render pass.

Because structs are value types, SwiftUI can efficiently diff
the old and new view trees to determine what actually changed
on screen. This is why views must be cheap to create.

Don't store heavy objects directly in your views. Instead, use
@StateObject or @EnvironmentObject for reference-type models
that need to survive view recreation.

Think of a SwiftUI view as a description of what should be on
screen, not the actual pixels. The framework handles rendering.

tips.title: @State, @Binding, and @ObservedObject explained
tips.content:
SwiftUI provides property wrappers to manage state and trigger
re-renders. Choosing the right one is critical.

@State is for simple, view-local value types (Int, String, Bool).
SwiftUI owns the storage and persists it across re-renders.
Mark it private — it belongs to that view only.

@Binding creates a two-way connection to state owned elsewhere.
The child view can read and write the parent's state without
owning it. Pass it with the $ prefix.

@ObservedObject watches an ObservableObject (reference type)
passed in from outside. When its @Published properties change,
the view re-renders. Don't create the object inside the view —
use @StateObject for that.

tips.title: Custom ViewModifiers for reusable styling
tips.content:
When you find yourself applying the same chain of modifiers
repeatedly, extract them into a custom ViewModifier. This
keeps your code DRY and consistent.

A ViewModifier is a struct with a body(content:) method that
wraps the original view with your modifications. You apply it
with .modifier() or a convenience extension on View.

ViewModifiers can have their own state, parameters, and even
animations. They compose naturally — you can stack multiple
custom modifiers just like built-in ones.

This pattern is especially powerful for design systems where
you want consistent card styles, button styles, or themed
text appearances across your entire app.
